**Draft benchmark PR. Do not merge intermediate commits.**

Seven sequential pushes, one sample each, measured on GitHub runners. The lockfile is constant across all seven so the only variable is the pytest configuration.

| commit | configuration |
|---|---|
| A1 | serial baseline (xdist pinned, unused) |
| A2 | serial repeat |
| B1 | `-n auto` |
| B2 | `-n auto` repeat |
| C1 | `-n auto --dist loadfile` |
| C2 | `-n auto --dist loadfile` repeat |
| D | winner only, rejected configurations reverted |

## Why seven and not four

`coverage` measured **111s** in the baseline and **129s** in the PR 1 run — 18s of runner variance on an unchanged job. That spread is larger than the entire PR 1 critical-path delta. One sample per configuration would be reading that noise, not xdist.

Two samples per configuration is the minimum that can separate a real ~50% pytest improvement from runner variance.

## Winner rule

Lowest **median** comparable critical-path time, only if every verification dimension is identical: test count, skipped, deselected, coverage result, threshold, evidence completeness, no flakiness, no unsafe AXLE load.

**Tie or indistinguishable → prefer serial.** No xdist for a marginal or theoretical gain.
**No meaningful median improvement → revert xdist and the lockfile, record `PERFORMANCE_REJECTED`.**

Learning that xdist does not help here is a successful experiment, not wasted runner time.

## Known hazard being measured

`tests/test_evidence.py:49` is a `scope="module"` fixture that shells out with a `timeout=300` budget. Under xdist's default `--dist load` it re-executes **once per worker**, which can make the suite slower. That is exactly what B vs C is for.
